difficultyReason: Stimulus presents quantitative medical data with a qualification about subgroups. Correct answer respects the hedge; traps drop a qualifier or overclaim causation.
stimulus: A ten-year study of patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes found that those who engaged in at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise per week showed, on average, a 0.8% reduction in hemoglobin A1c levels compared to those who did not exercise regularly. However, among patients who were also being treated with insulin, the reduction in A1c levels associated with exercise was less than 0.2% — a difference the study authors described as clinically negligible. The study did not examine whether exercise affected the required insulin dosages of patients in the insulin-treated group.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerobic exercise reduces hemoglobin A1c levels in all patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The benefit of aerobic exercise on blood glucose control may be smaller for insulin-treated diabetic patients than for those not on insulin therapy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin therapy eliminates the physiological mechanisms through which aerobic exercise improves blood glucose control.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physicians should not recommend aerobic exercise to patients who are being treated with insulin for Type 2 diabetes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ten-year study's findings establish that aerobic exercise is the most effective non-pharmacological intervention for managing Type 2 diabetes.

explanations.correct: The study shows a meaningful A1c reduction (0.8%) in non-insulin-treated patients but only a negligible reduction (0.2%) in insulin-treated patients. This directly supports the hedged claim that the benefit 'may be smaller' for insulin-treated patients — respecting the limitation that causation is not fully established.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus shows the benefit in insulin-treated patients is clinically negligible, so the claim that exercise reduces A1c 'in all patients' is not supported.
explanations.B: Correct — a hedged comparative claim that directly follows from the data contrast between the two subgroups.
explanations.C: Causal mechanism overreach — the study says nothing about whether insulin eliminates the physiological pathway; it only reports outcome data.
explanations.D: Policy prescription not supported — the stimulus explicitly does not examine all effects of exercise on insulin-treated patients (e.g., dosage changes), so a blanket recommendation against it is unwarranted.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the study compares exercise to no exercise, not to other non-pharmacological interventions, so no 'most effective' ranking is established.

difficultyReason: Economics stimulus with relative vs. absolute confusion as a key trap. Correct answer makes a hedged comparative claim; one distractor reads the relative data as absolute.
stimulus: Data from a regional housing authority covering 47 municipalities show that in municipalities where rent-stabilization ordinances were enacted between 2010 and 2015, the median monthly rent increased by 12 percent over the following five years. In municipalities in the same region that did not enact such ordinances during that period, median monthly rent increased by 31 percent over the same five years. The data do not indicate whether the municipalities that enacted ordinances had higher or lower baseline rents at the start of the period.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Renters in municipalities with rent-stabilization ordinances paid lower monthly rents than renters in municipalities without such ordinances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rent-stabilization ordinances caused rents to rise more slowly than they would have otherwise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the municipalities studied, the rate of rent increase was lower where rent-stabilization ordinances were in effect than where they were not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enacting rent-stabilization ordinances is the most reliable method for controlling rent increases in a municipality.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rent-stabilization ordinances benefit low-income renters more than they benefit middle-income renters.

explanations.correct: The data directly show a 12% increase in ordinance municipalities vs. 31% in non-ordinance municipalities — a straightforward comparative claim about rates of increase that the data plainly support.
explanations.A: Relative/absolute confusion trap — the data track rates of increase, not absolute rent levels. Without knowing baseline rents, we cannot say which group paid lower absolute amounts.
explanations.B: Causal overreach — the data show correlation; the stimulus does not rule out confounding variables that might explain the difference in growth rates.
explanations.D: Superlative overreach — 'most reliable method' implies a comparison with other methods, none of which are discussed in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Out of scope — income levels of renters are never mentioned in the stimulus.

difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a counterintuitive finding. The correct answer draws a modest inference from an apparent paradox; traps include opposite-direction and plausible-but-unsupported answers.
stimulus: Researchers monitoring a coastal estuary found that concentrations of nitrogen — a key nutrient for algal growth — increased significantly after a wetland restoration project was completed upstream. Despite this increase in nitrogen, algal bloom frequency in the estuary declined by approximately 30 percent over the three years following restoration, compared to the three years preceding it. Water salinity and temperature in the estuary remained stable across both periods.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Algal blooms in coastal estuaries are primarily caused by elevated water temperatures rather than by nitrogen concentrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wetland restoration project reduced algal bloom frequency by filtering nitrogen before it reached the estuary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nitrogen concentration is not the only factor that determines the frequency of algal blooms in the estuary studied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wetland restoration projects always reduce algal bloom frequency in nearby coastal estuaries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increases in nitrogen concentration generally lead to increases in algal bloom frequency in coastal estuaries.

explanations.correct: Nitrogen increased yet algal blooms declined — this directly demonstrates that nitrogen alone does not determine bloom frequency in this estuary. Some other factor must also be at work, so nitrogen is not the only determinant.
explanations.A: Too strong and unsupported — temperature remained stable across both periods, so it cannot explain the change; and 'primarily caused by' is an extreme, unsupported causal claim.
explanations.B: Causal mechanism overreach — the stimulus says nitrogen concentrations actually increased after restoration, making the claim that the project filtered nitrogen directly contradicted.
explanations.D: Scope creep with absolute language — 'always' and the generalization to 'all nearby coastal estuaries' far exceeds what one estuary's data can support.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data show nitrogen rose while blooms declined, which is the reverse of what this choice claims.

difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a controlled twist about a specific language subgroup diverging from a broader trend. Correct answer must scope correctly to that subgroup.
stimulus: A cross-linguistic survey of 94 languages found that the vast majority use word order as the primary means of conveying grammatical relationships between subjects and objects. However, among languages in the survey that employ an extensive system of morphological case markers — suffixes or prefixes attached to nouns to indicate their grammatical role — flexible word order was far more common than in languages lacking such a system. In the survey, no language with a fully fixed word order was found to also employ a comprehensive case-marking system.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Languages that rely on morphological case markers do not need word order to convey grammatical relationships.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the languages surveyed, having a comprehensive case-marking system was associated with greater flexibility in word order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All languages with flexible word order use morphological case markers to signal grammatical relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Morphological case-marking systems developed because early languages lacked fixed word-order rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Word order is a less reliable grammatical device than morphological case marking across all human languages.

explanations.correct: The survey directly shows that languages with extensive case-marking systems exhibited flexible word order far more commonly than those without — a hedged associative claim that stays within the scope of the survey data.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'do not need word order' is an absolute claim; the stimulus only says flexible order is more common, not that these languages abandon word order as a grammatical device entirely.
explanations.C: Reversal of direction — the data say case-marking languages tend to have flexible order, not that all flexible-order languages have case marking. This confuses the direction of the association.
explanations.D: Historical causal speculation — the stimulus presents synchronic survey data and makes no claims about historical development or causation.
explanations.E: 'Less reliable' and 'all human languages' both overreach; the stimulus makes a comparative frequency claim about a specific survey sample, not a universal evaluative ranking.

difficultyReason: Policy/law stimulus with statistical data on sentencing. Correct answer is a hedged comparative; traps include one that drops a crucial qualifier and one that makes an unsupported normative claim.
stimulus: A review of sentencing records in a state's superior courts from 2015 to 2022 found that defendants convicted of felony drug offenses who had retained private counsel received custodial sentences in 38 percent of cases. Defendants convicted of the same category of offenses who were represented by public defenders received custodial sentences in 61 percent of cases. The review controlled for the defendants' prior criminal records but did not control for the severity of the specific offense within the felony drug category.
questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Private attorneys are more skilled than public defenders at representing clients charged with drug offenses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among defendants with similar prior records convicted of felony drug offenses in the state studied, those with private counsel were less likely to receive custodial sentences than those with public defenders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The type of legal representation a defendant obtains is the primary determinant of the sentence imposed in felony drug cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Public defenders in the state studied are inadequately funded and overworked.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Defendants with private counsel receive lighter sentences than defendants with public defenders in all categories of criminal cases in the state.

explanations.correct: The review controlled for prior criminal records and found a 23-percentage-point gap in custodial sentence rates. The correct answer faithfully reflects what was controlled for ('similar prior records') and hedges appropriately ('less likely'), staying within the data's scope.
explanations.A: Plausible but unsupported — the data show an outcome difference but do not isolate attorney skill as the cause; offense severity was not controlled, and many other factors could explain the gap.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'primary determinant' implies this factor outweighs all others, which the data cannot establish since offense severity was not controlled.
explanations.D: Out of scope — resource levels and workload of public defenders are never mentioned; this is a plausible worldly belief not derivable from the stimulus.
explanations.E: Scope creep — the data cover only felony drug offenses; extending the conclusion to 'all categories of criminal cases' goes beyond what the review examined.

difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a surprising subgroup finding. Correct answer captures a hedged inference about a specific subgroup; traps include an absolute claim and an opposite-direction answer.
stimulus: An independent audit of a widely used algorithmic hiring tool found that the system's accuracy in predicting six-month job retention was 74 percent when evaluated across all applicants. However, for applicants who had gaps of 12 months or longer in their employment history, the algorithm's predictions were accurate only 51 percent of the time — barely above random chance. The audit noted that applicants with employment gaps constituted roughly 18 percent of the total applicant pool reviewed.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The algorithmic hiring tool performs less reliably for applicants with extended employment gaps than for the overall applicant pool.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Applicants with employment gaps of 12 months or longer are less likely to be retained for six months than applicants without such gaps.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The algorithm's overall accuracy of 74 percent is driven primarily by its strong performance on applicants without employment gaps.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Algorithmic hiring tools are inherently biased against applicants with non-traditional career histories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tool's predictions about applicants with employment gaps are more accurate than those about applicants without such gaps.

explanations.correct: 74% overall vs. 51% for the employment-gap subgroup directly supports the claim that the tool performs less reliably for that subgroup — a straightforward comparative inference from the numbers given.
explanations.B: Opposite direction / unsupported — the audit measures the accuracy of predictions about retention, not actual retention rates. Nothing in the stimulus says gap applicants are actually retained at lower rates.
explanations.C: Plausible but not fully supported — while mathematically plausible given the numbers and proportions, the stimulus does not provide the breakdown needed to confirm what 'drives' the overall accuracy; this requires calculation the stimulus does not invite.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — 'inherently biased' and 'algorithmic hiring tools' (plural, universal) go far beyond what one audit of one tool establishes.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the data show 51% accuracy for the gap subgroup versus 74% overall, so this choice directly inverts the finding.

difficultyReason: History stimulus with multiple data points across time periods. Correct answer makes a temporally scoped inference; a key trap extends the conclusion beyond the stated time period.
stimulus: Between 1880 and 1910, the proportion of the urban workforce in Western European industrializing cities employed in textile manufacturing declined from approximately 35 percent to 18 percent, while the proportion employed in metalworking and machine production rose from roughly 12 percent to 29 percent. Wages in metalworking averaged 40 percent higher than those in textile work throughout this period. Census records from the same cities indicate that average household income among urban factory workers increased modestly — by approximately 8 percent in real terms — over those three decades.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shift in employment from textiles to metalworking contributed to the modest rise in average household income among urban factory workers between 1880 and 1910.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Urban factory workers in Western Europe were better off economically in 1910 than at any other point in the nineteenth or twentieth centuries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Textile manufacturing was no longer an economically significant industry in Western European cities by 1910.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Workers who transferred from textile manufacturing to metalworking during this period each experienced a 40 percent increase in their personal wages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The growth of metalworking industries in Western European cities was caused by deliberate government policy during this period.

explanations.correct: Higher-wage metalworking employment expanded while lower-wage textile employment contracted, and household incomes rose modestly. It is strongly supported that the compositional shift contributed to the income rise — a hedged causal inference consistent with the direction and magnitude of the data.
explanations.B: Temporal scope creep — the data only cover 1880–1910; claiming workers were better off 'than at any other point' in both the nineteenth and twentieth centuries goes far beyond what these records establish.
explanations.C: Too strong — textile employment at 18% of the urban workforce still represents a substantial share; 'no longer economically significant' is not supported.
explanations.D: Misapplication of average to individuals — the 40% figure is an average sectoral wage difference, not a guarantee about individual worker outcomes; workers switching jobs might have entered at lower pay grades.
explanations.E: Causal overreach — government policy is never mentioned; attributing the industrial shift to deliberate policy introduces a cause the stimulus does not supply.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy stimulus presenting research on moral judgment with a qualification. Correct answer stays within the qualification; traps generalize improperly or introduce unsupported normative claims.
stimulus: Researchers presented participants with a series of moral dilemmas in which causing harm to one person would prevent greater harm to several others. Participants who had been asked to first perform arithmetic tasks solved correctly were significantly more likely to endorse harm-causing actions in these dilemmas than participants who had not done such tasks. The researchers noted, however, that this effect was observed only for dilemmas involving strangers — it did not appear when the potential harm target was described as a family member or close friend.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Performing arithmetic tasks causes people to reason more carefully about moral dilemmas in all contexts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Utilitarian moral reasoning is superior to other forms of moral reasoning for resolving dilemmas involving strangers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The effect of prior analytical activity on moral judgment may depend on the relationship between the judge and the potential harm target.

choices.label: D
choices.text: People who perform arithmetic tasks are more ethical than those who do not when confronting real-world moral dilemmas.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People are more likely to endorse causing harm to family members than to strangers in order to prevent greater overall harm.

explanations.correct: The study found the arithmetic-task effect only for stranger dilemmas, not for family/friend dilemmas — directly supporting the hedged claim that the effect of prior analytical activity on moral judgment may depend on the relationship between the judge and the target.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'in all contexts' contradicts the finding that the effect disappeared for family/friend dilemmas; the stimulus explicitly limits the effect's scope.
explanations.B: Normative overreach — the stimulus describes what participants endorsed, not which form of reasoning is 'superior'; normative ranking is not derivable from descriptive experimental data.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — being more likely to endorse a utilitarian trade-off in an abstract dilemma does not imply greater overall ethical behavior; 'more ethical' is a value judgment the stimulus does not support.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the effect (endorsing harm-causing actions) was observed for stranger dilemmas and not for family/friend dilemmas, so if anything the data suggest the reverse of this claim.

difficultyReason: Arts/economics stimulus with a counterintuitive revenue finding. Correct answer is a hedged inference about a specific market segment; traps include a too-strong generalization and a plausible-but-unsupported claim.
stimulus: A survey of 200 independent recording artists who released albums between 2018 and 2023 found that artists who made their music available exclusively through paid-download platforms generated average annual revenues of approximately $4,200 from recorded music. Artists who made their music available for free streaming in addition to paid downloads generated average annual revenues of approximately $7,800 — nearly double — from recorded music during the same period. The survey excluded artists signed to major record labels and did not measure revenue from live performances or merchandise.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For at least some independent recording artists, making music available for free streaming is associated with higher recorded-music revenue than relying solely on paid downloads.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free streaming platforms increase total revenue for all musicians, including those signed to major record labels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Independent recording artists should always distribute their music through free streaming platforms rather than relying exclusively on paid downloads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recorded-music industry as a whole generates more revenue from free streaming than from paid downloads.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Independent artists who use free streaming earn more from live performances and merchandise than those who rely only on paid downloads.

explanations.correct: The survey data show that the free-streaming group averaged nearly double the revenue of the paid-download-only group. The hedged 'for at least some' phrasing correctly captures that these are averages across surveyed independent artists, without overclaiming universality.
explanations.B: Scope creep — the survey explicitly excluded major-label artists; extending the finding to 'all musicians including those signed to major labels' goes beyond the data.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'should always' is a prescriptive absolute; the survey shows averages, not a universal relationship, and individual circumstances could differ substantially.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the survey measured individual artist revenues, not industry-wide totals; and the comparison between streaming and paid-download revenue in aggregate is not addressed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the survey explicitly did not measure live performance or merchandise revenue, so no inference about those income streams is possible.

difficultyReason: Environmental science / policy stimulus with data on conservation outcomes. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference; traps include causal overreach and a temporal scope error.
stimulus: An analysis of 63 marine protected areas (MPAs) established worldwide between 1990 and 2005 found that fish biomass within MPA boundaries was, on average, 2.3 times greater than in comparable unprotected areas of the same ocean regions after 15 years of protection. The analysis also found, however, that MPAs established in regions with active pre-existing enforcement of fishing regulations showed a biomass ratio of only 1.4 — substantially lower than the overall average. MPAs established in regions with little prior regulatory enforcement showed a biomass ratio of 3.1.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marine protected areas are the most effective conservation tool available for rebuilding depleted ocean fish populations globally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish biomass in unprotected ocean areas will decline relative to that in MPAs for as long as MPAs remain in force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The magnitude of the fish biomass increase associated with MPA establishment tends to be greater in regions where pre-existing fishing regulations were weakly enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Establishing an MPA causes fish populations to recover more rapidly in regions with weak prior enforcement than in regions with strong prior enforcement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In regions with active pre-existing enforcement of fishing regulations, establishing an MPA provides no meaningful conservation benefit.

explanations.correct: The data directly show a biomass ratio of 3.1 in low-enforcement regions vs. 1.4 in high-enforcement regions — a clear pattern supporting the hedged claim that biomass gains 'tend to be greater' where prior enforcement was weak.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope — 'most effective conservation tool globally' compares MPAs to all other possible tools, none of which are discussed in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Temporal scope creep — the study covers a specific 15-year window; projecting that the trend will continue 'for as long as MPAs remain in force' extrapolates beyond the data.
explanations.D: Causal overreach — the data show a correlation between prior enforcement levels and biomass ratios, but do not establish that MPA establishment itself causes more rapid recovery; baseline conditions could explain much of the difference.
explanations.E: Too strong — a ratio of 1.4 still represents a 40% greater biomass within MPAs compared to unprotected areas, which constitutes a meaningful difference; 'no meaningful benefit' is contradicted by the data.
